extracted.intended_audience: regulators, agency counsel, environmental lawyers, and public commenters preparing legal comments on EPA rulemakings (notice-and-comment submissions)
extracted.subtask_description: Drafting or evaluating formal legal comments to an EPA notice-and-comment rulemaking contesting the Agency's interpretation of the Clean Air Act, particularly regarding Section 202 authority over greenhouse gases. Emphasizes statutory interpretation, stare decisis, administrative practice, and doctrinal limits (UARG, CRA, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross‑sectional statutory ratification
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress’s explicit ratification of EPA’s authority over greenhouse gases under one provision (e.g., Section 111) serves to affirm EPA’s authority over that same pollutant under the same terms in another provision (e.g., Section 202).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use evidence that Congress ratified EPA authority in related provisions to support the same reading elsewhere; explain that nearly identical statutory language across sections should be treated consistently. Example text: 'Congress’s explicit ratification of EPA’s authority over greenhouse gases under Section 111 serves to affirm EPA’s authority ... under Section 202.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized provisions do not negate general authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The existence of a special provision addressing a pollutant (e.g., waste methane) does not imply that EPA lacks authority to regulate that pollutant under the Act’s general standard‑setting provisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argue that EPA may regulate pollutants under general category standards even where the Act contains separate, specialized provisions; provide examples (VOCs regulated under Section 202 and Section 111 despite Section 183 and Section 112).

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentive or voluntary programs do not preclude regulatory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional creation of incentive or voluntary programs to reduce emissions does not logically preclude EPA from exercising regulatory authority over the same pollutants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish sticks and carrots; show provisions that 'affirmatively support EPA’s authority' (e.g., funding directing EPA to achieve reductions 'through use of the existing authorities of this Act'). Cite examples like Section 135/7435 and Section 136.

rubrics_metrics.name: Budgetary rescissions do not repeal substantive statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: A budgetary statute that rescinds unobligated balances or delays collection (e.g., a reconciliation act) does not, by itself, restrict or repeal an agency’s substantive statutory authority unless it amends the operative statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain that rescinding funds or delaying collection of a charge does not alter the underlying statutory command; cite examples of rescinded unobligated balances and the continued existence of unamended statutory text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeal of program-specific definitions does not change statutory meaning elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeal of a now‑defunct, program‑specific definition (e.g., in a repealed grant program) does not demonstrate congressional disagreement with the underlying conceptual definition used elsewhere in the statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Show that a program's repeal renders that program-specific definition obsolete but leaves identical definitions in other provisions undisturbed; caution against inferring intent to alter general statutory terms from program repeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional Review Act disapproval does not abrogate statutory authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Disapproval under the Congressional Review Act invalidates a particular rulemaking approach but does not change the underlying statutory command or the agency’s authority granted by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish invalidation of a rule from repeal of statutory power; cite 5 U.S.C. § 801(b)(2) (bar on promulgating a 'substantially the same' rule) and note that statutory authority remains intact even if a specific rule is disapproved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect for statutory stare decisis and special justification requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: An agency cannot lawfully base action on the premise that controlling Supreme Court precedent should be overturned; departing from statutory precedent requires a 'special justification' and consideration of established factors for overruling.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an agency's interpretation depends on overruling Supreme Court precedent, it must address the considerations for departing from stare decisis (e.g., quality of precedent’s reasoning, workability, reliance interests, congressional failure to correct). Cite Kimble, Loper, Janus, Patterson, Kisor, and explain the elevated burden when seeking to overturn a long line of precedents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not assume Massachusetts can be disregarded without explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: Because Massachusetts unambiguously treated greenhouse gases as 'air pollutants' under Section 202, an agency must not proceed on an implicit premise that that precedent no longer governs without substantiating why it should be overturned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require the agency to demonstrate how factors justifying overruling apply; note that mere prognostication that the Court might overturn is insufficient and unlawful as a basis for rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Textual reading: 'any air pollutant' is expansive
rubrics_metrics.description: The plain‑text meaning of 'any' is expansive; Section 202(a)’s grant to regulate 'any air pollutant' supports a broad authority that includes greenhouse gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply ordinary meaning canons (e.g., 'any' = 'one or some indiscriminately of whatever kind') and cite supporting cases (Dep’t of HUD v. Rucker, J.E.M. AG Supply). Use the statutory text as a primary anchor for authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use statutory definitions (Section 302(g)) as controlling
rubrics_metrics.description: Congress’s definitional provisions—e.g., Section 302(g)’s definition of 'air pollutant'—should be treated as virtually conclusive in construing the same terms elsewhere in the Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rely on the statute’s own definition that lists 'any air pollution agent ... including any physical, chemical ... substance' and expressly includes precursors; argue that greenhouse gases fall within that definition and that courts normally give such definitions controlling weight (Sturgeon v. Frost).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contextual definitions (e.g., 'welfare') support inclusion of climate harms
rubrics_metrics.description: Contextual statutory definitions—such as Section 302(h)’s inclusion of 'effects on ... weather ... and climate' in 'welfare'—confirm that greenhouse gas emissions fit within the harms the Act was designed to address.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use cross‑references to statutory definitions of harms and welfare to show Congress intended the Act to encompass climate impacts; argue it would be nonsensical to exclude the primary pollutant threatening climate when assessing contributions to dangerous air pollution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative practice and historical positions matter
rubrics_metrics.description: EPA’s prior consistent positions, rulemakings, findings, and decades of practice recognizing greenhouse gases as air pollutants buttress the interpretation that Section 202 encompasses greenhouse gases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cite historical documents, memoranda, testimony (e.g., 1998 Cannon memo, 1999 testimony), rulemakings (2010, 2012, 2016, etc.), denials of petitions to reconsider, and court outcomes to show long‑standing agency understanding and reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: UARG inapposite absent absurd regulatory consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility Air Regulatory Group (UARG) reasoning that supported a narrower meaning in other statutory contexts is distinguishable where applying the statutory definition would not produce the kind of absurd or unworkable regulatory consequences (e.g., massive expansion via numeric thresholds) that drove UARG.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate that Section 202 lacks the UARG problem (no automatic numeric thresholds triggering unmanageable expansion), so UARG does not justify narrowing 'air pollutant' in Section 202. Cite UARG’s limiting rationale and contrast with Section 202’s structure and predicate findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption that identical statutory words bear the same meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: Identical words and phrases within the same statute should normally be given the same meaning; deviation is justified only where applying the uniform definition would be incompatible with the statute’s scheme or would destroy a major purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invoke Powerex and related authority; require showing that the presumption must yield (e.g., unworkability, absurdity) before construing the term differently in a particular section.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid surplusage and favor constructions that render statutory design effective
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations should avoid surplusage and should favor readings that make the statutory design effective and facilitate the policies behind enactment rather than making them more difficult to fulfill.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use canons against surplusage (Fischer, Montclair) and purposive reasoning (Nat'l Petroleum Refiners Ass'n) to prefer constructions that give effect to all statutory provisions and avoid rendering language meaningless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for Section 202’s interposed limitations and feasibility constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Section 202 contains predicate criteria (finding of contribution to dangerous air pollution) and procedural/feasibility considerations (lead time, costs) that constrain and modulate EPA’s exercise of its broad authority, preventing the regulatory absurdities UARG feared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When defending a broad reading of 'air pollutant,' explain how Section 202’s substantive and procedural checks (endangerment finding, feasibility/lead time considerations) ensure manageable application and avoid the need to carve out globally dispersed pollutants.
